newsitem.title: USA: Woolworth mulls transforming general stores.
newsitem.headline: Woolworth mulls transforming general stores.

text.p: Woolworth Corp is considering closing or converting more than half its troubled 410 general merchandise stores, once America's favorite five & dimes, Wall Street analysts said.

The stores have been losing money and sapping Woolworth's bottom line. A report Wednesday by CNBC said the retailer "is close" to announcing it may sublet some stores, while others could be converted into Foot Lockers, the successul footwear division of Woolworth. Many could close.
A Woolworth spokesman, responding to the report, said the company does not comment on "rumors and speculation".
Woolworth chairman Roger Farah told investors in June that the firm would consider selling stores in the division after disappointing first quarter sales, analysts said.

The U.S. general merchandise stores had first-quarter sales of $224 million, less than last year's $244 million. That contributed about 12.6 percent to Woolworth's top line of $1.77 billion in total first quarter revenues.
The retailer recently installed new technology and computer systems at the stores to improve efficiencies.
Woolworth had wanted to see how the division's performance stood at year-end, but analysts said the first quarter results were disappointing.

"(Woolworth) said the stores were still losing money ... and they would take a look at the end of the year. If they didn't meet their requirements, they would bite the bullet," said Standard & Poor's analyst Karen Sack.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Jeffrey Feiner last month upgraded the stock, saying the potential closing of some domestic stores gave the stock some appeal.
Citicorp Securities analyst Margaret Cannella said: "If they don't make money, it's a good idea to sell. But I'm not sure they're going to make that decision right now."
Another Woolworth analyst, Otto Grote of Derby Securities, said Woolworth could not get rid of the chain fast enough.
"I don't know what took them so long," said Grote. He noted that some of the stores have excellent leases because they were negotiated in the 1940's.
